chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
title: Lalo Schifrin, Dizzy and film work for black musicians
summary: Mingus's paranoia about black players excluded from films and TV; Johnson disagrees about Schifrin.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Maybe that's why I'm crippled now, man, all that religious fear and stuff, man. I don't think anything is really wrong with me. I think I'm having an extreme paranoia illusion. The world's against me, as a black man. I know that, not the world, but the profession I'm in. Hasn't grown up yet.
What's this piano player used to be with Dizzy Gillespie? That makes a lot of movies now.
I mean, he's bigger than Dizzy Gillespie, his future is made. And Dizzy can write.
Dizzy don't get no television jobs, no movies.
Yeah, but Lallo -- I don't think it's anything to do with the fact that Lallo wasn't black. I just

think that Lallo had a natural bent. He wasn't a very good -- he couldn't swing to save his ass. He had a terrible time rushing, something awful. But he knew how to write some of that bullshit music that they like for television. And so he did that. But Dizzy's a bigger man than Lallo Schiffer is ever going to be.
Dizzy must make a lot of money just on royalties from his tunes. How many recordings of Night in Tunisia are there, and how many recordings of --
Jazz guys? They don't sell no records.
They sell enough so that he makes a damn decent taste.
I'll ask him sometime. I doubt it.
